This paper introduces Suryakala-Nusantara, a pioneering digital humanities project that catalogs Indonesian sundials through an innovative, collaborative approach. By integrating digital technology with cultural heritage, this project aims to create a comprehensive database of Indonesian sundials, thereby preserving and promoting the unique timekeeping traditions of the region.

This research introduces a cutting-edge D2D communication model that incorporates an RIS and integrated access and backhaul (IAB) nodes, with the goal of optimizing a complex system. The study focuses on maximizing the sum data rate of D2D links by jointly adjusting the RIS configuration, D2D transmission power, and scheduling. The problem is divided into two manageable sub-problems, with the first involving optimizing the RIS configuration and the second focusing on power control and scheduling. The results show that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms existing benchmarks in terms of data rate and power efficiency.

This paper outlines a novel approach to operating a single LDV system in a two-dimensional measurement mode by remotely controlling the beam-steering mirror. By strategically positioning the beam-steering mirror, researchers can obtain velocity data in two spatial dimensions. The effectiveness of this method was demonstrated through a comparative study involving simultaneous measurements using both one and three LDV beam-steering setups, revealing that the two-dimensional measurement method yields results comparable to those of the traditional three-dimensional setup.

We establish that the collection of all possible spectrum sets from first-order theories featuring only binary relations is countable and can be systematically identified through a specific, identifiable subset.

A programmable phase plate is a device that can be controlled electronically to modify the electron wave, and it is becoming an essential tool in advanced transmission electron microscopy. Traditionally, it has been used to enhance image quality by modifying the contrast, but our research demonstrates that it can also correct distortions in the electron beam, thereby improving the microscope's overall performance. By conducting a detailed analysis of the electron beam's properties, we found that specific patterns on the phase plate can effectively correct various types of distortions, including those caused by misalignments and imperfections in the microscope's lenses. Our findings show that the phase plate can correct these distortions with high precision, and it has the potential to be a valuable addition to modern transmission electron microscopes.

This paper explores the fundamental connection between measurement and computation, revealing that measurement is essentially a specific form of computation. We establish a general framework for measurement, demonstrating its applicability across various contexts, including quantum mechanics. Furthermore, our framework enables the development of measurement update rules, which are shown to be consistent with established quantum update methods.

We examine the set of points in the integer grid of $d$ dimensions that can be reached by a random walker starting from the origin, given a maximum number of steps $n$. The points are defined by their $L_1$-norm, which is the sum of the absolute values of their $d$ coordinates. The problem involves calculating the probability that a random walker will be at a specific point after $n$ steps, and we provide a formula for this probability in terms of $n$ and the dimensions of the space.

In this research, we delve into the intricacies of the extended model of the black hole, specifically focusing on the recently proposed polymer black hole by Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin. By applying the extended model, we resolve the issue of the singularity within the black hole, and further, we demonstrate that the transition from the classical to the polymer black hole can be represented through a geometric framework. Furthermore, we investigate the properties of the quasinormal modes of the black hole, and our findings reveal that the real part of the quasinormal frequencies exhibits a linear relationship with the Planck length, while the imaginary part displays an inverse relationship with the Planck length.

We have derived a general formula for the dynamic screening function in doped graphene at finite temperatures using the random phase approximation. This finding allows us to calculate the specific heat of the material and reveals that at low temperatures, the specific heat is linearly proportional to temperature, with a coefficient that is directly related to the material's carrier density. This relationship holds true for undoped graphene as well, where the specific heat coefficient is approximately 10^-4 mJ/K^2 per gram.

This paper introduces MaskedSpeech, a novel approach to speech synthesis that incorporates a masking strategy inspired by the success of masked language modeling in NLP. By leveraging contextual information, MaskedSpeech significantly enhances the quality of speech output, particularly in terms of intelligibility and acoustic accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that MaskedSpeech outperforms existing methods, including a fully connected baseline and a transformer-based model, with notable improvements in speech quality and automatic speech recognition accuracy.

We introduce a novel Bayesian projection predictive approach that leverages the
latent space of deep generative models for predictive purposes. By projecting
predictions made on observed data into the latent space and sampling from the
resulting distribution, our method offers an efficient approximation of predictive
distributions. We evaluate the performance of this approach using both simulated
and real-world data, comparing it to alternative predictive techniques.

Recent breakthroughs in machine learning have led to its widespread adoption in classification tasks, but this has also made it a prime target for adversaries. In response to this growing threat, researchers have developed various defenses against machine learning classification attacks. However, these studies have primarily focused on scenarios where the attacker has full control over the data generation process. In this paper, we investigate a new type of attack that takes place in a scenario where the data is generated by a model that is not under the attacker's control. We introduce a new class of attacks that take place in a scenario where the data is generated by a model that is not under the attacker's control. We show that these attacks are particularly effective against state-of-the-art machine learning classification models. We also introduce a new type of defense that is based on the principle of robustness and is able to withstand these attacks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed attacks and defenses through extensive experiments on real-world datasets.

Climate change conspiracy theories are a significant issue that undermines the public's understanding of the climate crisis. To address this, we conducted a study to examine the prevalence and characteristics of such theories on social media platforms. By analyzing 1,000 English-language tweets from 2019 to 2020, we identified 102 conspiracy theory-related keywords and found that 1,000 tweets contained climate change conspiracy theory content. Our results indicate that such content is often disseminated by individuals who are not well-informed about the climate crisis and who tend to express their views in a negative and dismissive manner. We also found that such content is often shared by individuals who are not well-informed about the climate crisis and who tend to express their views in a negative and dismissive manner. We discuss the implications of these findings and suggest potential strategies for addressing climate change conspiracy theories on social media.

A search for dark matter in association with top quarks is conducted using data from 13 TeV proton-proton collisions. The dataset, with a total luminosity of 137 fb^-1, is analyzed to identify potential dark matter signals in events containing a top quark and various final states indicative of dark matter. The analysis is based on the assumption that dark matter is produced in conjunction with a top quark or a top quark pair, and that its presence is signalled by an imbalance in transverse momentum. The results are presented in the form of 95% confidence level limits on the production cross-section of dark matter in association with top quarks, using the framework of simplified models featuring a mediator particle.

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based subcategories. Additionally, we demonstrate a one-to-one correspondence between the duality in question and the presence of a specific type of duality within the category.

This paper presents a statistical framework for analyzing instrumental variables that influence multiple treatment options in a non-linear manner. It derives conditions under which these instruments can be considered valid in the context of data that is not continuous. Using this framework, the study evaluates the impact of fields of study on graduates' salaries and finds that the returns to fields of study are not linear and are significantly different from each other.

The J/psi factory offers a unique opportunity to produce rare particles like antiprotons in high quantities, enabling groundbreaking experiments. This capability is set to yield significant advancements in understanding the fundamental properties of matter and the intricate workings of the universe.

In a study of triple star systems, researchers examined how the presence of a companion star affects the flow of material from a central binary system. They found that the presence of a companion star can cause the central binary to spin faster or slower, which in turn affects the rate at which material is transferred between the stars. This effect is more pronounced when the companion star is far away, and it can be used to explain the unusual properties of certain binary systems.

We examine flat, intrinsically cosmological models within a crystalline lattice structure, where the lattice's symmetry is used to derive the Einstein equations in a simplified form. Our analysis reveals that the resulting matter content is consistent with a cosmological model, characterized by anisotropic expansion rates in different directions. Furthermore, we find that the model's intrinsically flat nature is preserved, and its properties are influenced by the lattice's geometry and symmetry.

A novel approach to image segmentation is introduced, which incorporates a previously established image restoration model. By leveraging the proven image restoration capabilities, this method enhances segmentation performance. The proposed variational model is supported by both theoretical and empirical findings. Specifically, the existence of minimizers is proven, along with the development of efficient minimization algorithms. Furthermore, the convergence of these algorithms is demonstrated, and their practical effectiveness is validated through numerical experiments.

Heavy quasars can rapidly spin up due to an energy transfer process called superradiance, which occurs when they interact with certain types of ultralight particles. This interaction causes the particles to form a dense cloud around the black hole, which in turn slows its rotation. We've developed a method to estimate the mass range of these particles based on the observed spins of heavy quasars, and our analysis suggests that their masses may fall within a specific range.

The recent Loihi chip by Intel is a cutting-edge piece of hardware that can mimic the workings of the human brain. Its advanced design allows for highly efficient processing of complex neural networks, making it an ideal candidate for developing AI applications. To facilitate the development of such applications, Intel has created a specialized programming language called SpiNNaker Machine Interface (SpikeML). However, this language is not widely accessible and has limited support for advanced neural models. To overcome these limitations, we have developed an innovative solution - an emulator called Brian2Loihi. This innovative tool integrates with the widely-used neural network simulator, known as Brian, to provide a more accessible programming interface for Loihi. By combining the strengths of Brian and Loihi, our emulator allows researchers and developers to design and test complex neural models with greater ease and efficiency.

A solar noise storm is a phenomenon that arises from the dynamic evolution of a compact magnetic field source, which is often associated with the release of energy in the form of flares. To gain a deeper understanding of the underlying physical processes, researchers have developed a technique to track the evolution of this magnetic field source using radio observations. By analyzing a series of observations made during a microflare event, researchers found that the size of the source increased significantly, while its location remained relatively stable. Furthermore, they discovered that the magnetic field strength within the source decreased gradually, which is consistent with the release of energy in the form of a flare. These findings provide valuable insights into the complex dynamics of magnetic field evolution in the solar atmosphere, and may help to shed light on the fundamental processes that drive solar flares.

A magneto-optical trap has been successfully created on a two-dimensional integrated platform, combining a 200 nm thick YIG film with a 500 nm thick GaAs film. The YIG film's magnetization was manipulated using a microstrip antenna to generate a 279.8 MHz microwave signal, while a 532 nm laser was focused onto a magneto-optical cavity formed by the YIG and GaAs films. The cavity's transmitted light was then passed through a 585 nm Rb beam, which was magnetically deflected and focused onto the Rb atoms using a quadrupole magnetic field generated by a nearby current-carrying wire. The experiment demonstrated a significant increase in the transmitted light intensity, indicating the presence of Rb atoms in the magneto-optical trap.

The impact of angular momentum on the steady-state accretion of a collisional gas onto a non-rotating black hole, surrounded by a hot, ionized medium, is examined. This analysis is based on a model that assumes the gas originates from a spherical boundary at a finite distance from the black hole. It is found that the mass accretion rate is significantly influenced by the angular momentum of the gas, particularly when the boundary is located at a considerable distance from the black hole. This is due to the fact that the gas with higher angular momentum tends to orbit at a greater distance from the black hole, reducing the likelihood of it falling in. This effect is particularly pronounced when the angular momentum of the gas is close to the critical value required for it to orbit at the innermost stable circular orbit. This analysis also reveals that the mass accretion rate is significantly lower than previously estimated in models that assume the gas originates at the event horizon of the black hole. This is particularly relevant for understanding the accretion processes in systems such as X-ray binaries and active galactic nuclei.

The interaction between a two-level atom and the vacuum fluctuations of the electromagnetic field is examined, specifically when the atom is in a state of rest or in uniform motion near a perfectly conducting mirror. The analysis reveals that the motion can induce atomic excitation and spontaneous emission, which is heavily influenced by the direction of motion relative to the mirror. Furthermore, the motion-induced emission is found to be significantly amplified when the atom is in a state of rest, with the effect becoming even more pronounced in the presence of the mirror.

A recent study of the massive star population surrounding the young cluster Westerlund 2 has been conducted. Spectral analysis of 10 massive stars revealed that 8 of them are located in the cluster's outskirts. The spectral features of these stars were compared to models of stars with masses ranging from 15 to 30 solar masses. The analysis showed that Westerlund 2 contains a significant number of massive stars, including 10 O-type stars and one Wolf-Rayet star. The cluster's massive star population is estimated to be around 100 solar masses, with a mass function that is similar to other young clusters. The analysis also revealed that Westerlund 2 contains a significant number of massive stars that are not located in the cluster's core. The presence of these stars suggests that Westerlund 2 may have formed in a larger, more extended cluster that has since dispersed.

This study investigates a specific type of fourth-order nonlinear Schrödinger equation, which incorporates a nonlinear interaction term with an extreme growth rate. We demonstrate the existence of normalized ground states for this equation, leveraging a combination of concentration-compactness principles and minimization techniques on a specially designed manifold.

Degraded document images, often encountered in historical and archival contexts, can be effectively enhanced using image enhancement techniques. However, these methods sometimes distort the original content, making them unsuitable for accurate reading. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a novel approach that combines multiple tasks within a single network to improve the quality of degraded document images. This approach utilizes a multi-task adversarial network that incorporates both image enhancement and a perceptual matching task to preserve the original content. Furthermore, we have introduced a new dataset, EnhanceDRID, consisting of 1,000 pairs of degraded and corresponding original document images, to facilitate the evaluation of our method. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms existing methods in terms of image enhancement quality and content preservation.

The increasing use of digital data has led to a surge in digitization efforts, 
with organizations seeking to convert physical documents into digital format. 
This research introduces an automated system for extracting information from 
Indonesian identification cards using advanced optical character recognition 
technology. The proposed method combines OCR with natural language processing 
to enhance accuracy and efficiency. By leveraging deep learning models and 
Indonesian language resources, the system achieves a character-level accuracy 
of 90.1% and word-level accuracy of 81.1% on a custom dataset of 1000 ID card 
images.

This research introduces a novel, efficient method for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p networks, leveraging the existing preamble structure and employing a long LSTM model. The proposed approach utilizes a short training sequence to generate initial estimates, which are then refined through a temporal averaging process. The outcome is a more accurate channel estimation with reduced complexity, which is further validated through simulation experiments.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have significantly impacted the field of astronomy, particularly in image processing. This paper outlines a novel approach to enhancing low-resolution astronomical images through colorization and resolution improvement using generative adversarial networks. The proposed method leverages the power of deep learning to generate realistic and detailed images, which can aid astronomers in their research.

We introduce a novel, versatile neural network architecture grounded in the universal approximation theorem. This theorem enables the approximation of any continuous function through a combination of ReLU and its shifted counterpart, 1+ReLU. By leveraging this principle, we can decompose complex functions into manageable components, each represented by a network unit. Our approach offers a simplified alternative to conventional gradient-based training methods, utilizing a more intuitive optimization process. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of this framework through its application to regression and classification tasks.

Established in 2011, the ECR Panel has been instrumental in organizing workshops, conferences, and other events to foster collaboration and knowledge exchange among its members. In 2021-2022, the ECR Panel was led by a new chair, who took over from the previous term. The new chair, along with the panel's vice-chair and secretary, oversaw the panel's activities, which included the organization of workshops, conferences, and other events. The panel's activities were focused on promoting the careers of young researchers, providing them with opportunities for professional development, and fostering collaboration and knowledge exchange among its members. A newly designed optical metasurface enables the manipulation of line waves in free space, utilizing two layers of the metasurface to convert and redirect the waves. The first layer transforms a line wave into a focused beam, which then interacts with the second layer to produce a desired output wave pattern. The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated through numerical simulations, showcasing the ability to produce complex wave patterns such as rotated and split line waves.

This research paper outlines a pioneering approach to large-scale collaborative learning between humans and robots, utilizing a cognitive architecture that integrates the GAMA, SOAR, and Deep Q-Learning frameworks. The proposed system enables a group of robots and humans to learn complex tasks through repeated interactions, with the ability to adapt to new tasks and incorporate novel knowledge. The study's findings demonstrate the feasibility of this approach in achieving high levels of collaboration and learning within a short timeframe.

A bias-corrected estimator for the mean absolute deviation from the median is developed and evaluated in a finite sample context. The bias-corrected estimator outperforms its non-corrected counterpart, exhibiting reduced variability and improved accuracy. The bias correction method is then applied to create a more precise confidence interval for the mean absolute deviation from the median, which is subsequently evaluated through simulation studies.

This study explores the connection between two tasks: identifying relationships in texts and adding missing information to a database of interconnected entities. We investigate how these tasks can inform and improve each other, and develop a unified model that accomplishes both. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its superior performance on a widely-used dataset for identifying relationships in texts.

In this research, we investigate the quasi-particle Debye mass in an N-dimensional space, considering finite baryonic chemical potential and momentum anisotropy. By applying the hard thermal loop approximation, we derive the quasi-particle Debye mass in the N-dimensional space, taking momentum anisotropy and finite baryonic chemical potential into account. Furthermore, we examine the impact of momentum anisotropy and finite baryonic chemical potential on the quasi-particle Debye mass in the N-dimensional space. Additionally, we analyze the dissociation properties of quarkonia in the N-dimensional space, considering the effects of momentum anisotropy and finite baryonic chemical potential.

The compound exhibits two types of Ru spins, with one set aligned in the ab plane and the other perpendicular to it. The Ru spins are arranged in chains along the c axis, with alternating bond directions. The Ru spins are influenced by a magnetic field that varies in direction and strength, causing them to orient in different directions. The Ru spins are also influenced by the magnetic properties of the Tb ions, which are influenced by the temperature. Deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks, have been highly effective in image processing tasks, but their ability to generalize across different types of images is limited. This is largely due to the fact that the activation patterns of the convolutional layers are not well-suited for capturing complex, hierarchical features in natural images. To address this issue, we have developed a new approach that combines a self-attention mechanism with a Fourier transformation to create a more versatile representation of local image features. This method, called Modulated Periodic Activations (MPA), is based on the idea that the convolutional layers can be viewed as a series of modulated periodic filters, which can be used to capture a broader range of features in the image. By using this approach, we have been able to achieve significant improvements in the performance of deep learning models on a variety of image processing tasks, including image classification, semantic segmentation, and super-resolution.

We introduce semi-generative models that integrate both generative and discriminative components, enabling the analysis of covariate-shift scenarios involving causal and non-causal data attributes. This novel framework is exemplified by the semi-Gaussian model, which is shown to be adaptable to various distributions through the use of latent variables and semi-generative mixtures. A novel method for identifying causal data attributes is developed, along with a novel approach for adjusting these data attributes to accommodate covariate shifts. This approach is further illustrated through the application of semi-gaussian models to real-world data sets, including the MNIST and CelebA data sets.

This study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of deep learning's underlying principles, focusing on the geometric aspects of its operation. We will examine the connections between deep learning and manifold learning, as well as the role of geometric transformations in convolutional neural networks. Furthermore, we will explore the implications of spectral learning and the influence of data distribution on deep learning's success.

This paper demonstrates that Principal Factor Analysis can be reformulated as a low-rank matrix completion problem, which is then addressed by leveraging the lattice structure inherent in the data to develop an efficient algorithm for finding the minimum lattice points, thereby providing a solution to the problem.

The growing complexity of machine learning models has led to a pressing need for their interpretability, especially in high-energy physics applications. To address this, researchers have developed various techniques to make black-box models more transparent. This study focuses on two methods: one that incorporates domain-specific features into neural networks and another that analyzes the relevance of network components to its output. By applying these techniques to a jet tagging problem, we aim to gain insights into the strengths and weaknesses of each approach.

For a given positive integer r, the r-associated Stirling numbers of the first kind, denoted as $\left[ \begin{matrix} n \\ k \end{matrix} \right]_r$, count the number of ways to arrange n items into k non-empty groups, where each group contains at least r items. These numbers are related to ordinary Stirling numbers when r equals 1. Researchers have explored various properties of these numbers and their applications in combinatorics.

This research involves developing layer groups, their associated symmetry operations, and relevant mathematical representations, specifically focusing on the double cover groups of 11 particular single and double gray layer groups.

We examine the Lie algebra of momentum operators derived from Killing vectors on Riemannian manifolds, specifically focusing on those with geodesic flow. This subgroup's properties are analyzed in relation to the full algebra of momentum operators, with an emphasis on its structural composition.

A significant computational barrier in quantum Monte Carlo simulations is the Hubbard sign problem, which severely restricts the accuracy of results. To overcome this issue, we have developed a novel approach that utilizes complex-valued neural networks to develop an efficient approximation of the Hubbard action weight. This method enables us to transform the sign problem into a manageable sampling issue, which can be effectively addressed. Our results demonstrate that this approach yields precise outcomes for the Hubbard model at low temperatures and high interaction strengths, areas typically affected by the sign problem.

A new class of models, combining composite Higgs and flavon features, is proposed. These models utilize two types of flavons, which interact with the Higgs doublet through a global symmetry, to generate the observed Higgs mass and mixing angle. The model's framework is initially outlined, followed by a detailed examination of its implications for the Higgs sector, as well as its predictions for the flavor sector and composite physics.

Virtual reality technology has the potential to artificially alter human perception, which could lead to unintended negative consequences. Research indicates that VR can modify sensory experiences, including the perception of size, weight, and distance, by manipulating sensory inputs. This capability raises concerns about the possible misuse of VR to manipulate human perception, which could lead to the exploitation of users for financial gain or the infliction of psychological harm. Furthermore, the implications of such manipulation extend beyond individual users to society as a whole, potentially leading to the erosion of trust in VR technology and the development of harmful societal norms.

We investigate the potential of fine-tuning large language models on languages they were not originally trained on, using a minimal amount of data. Our experiments with BigScience's large multilingual model reveal that it can be effectively adapted to new languages, such as Georgian, with surprisingly little data. Notably, the model's performance on adapted languages is comparable to that of a model specifically trained on a single language, with the added benefit of requiring significantly less data. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the model's ability to be adapted to new languages is influenced by the presence of related languages in its training data.

The process of star formation is a complex and dynamic phenomenon, with binary systems being a significant outcome. To understand the factors influencing the masses of these systems, a numerical simulation was conducted, modeling the collapse of a rotating cloud core. By gradually increasing the mass of the core, researchers were able to observe the formation of binary systems and analyze the relationship between the core's mass and the masses of the resulting stars. The results showed that binary systems form when the core's mass exceeds a certain threshold, with the masses of the resulting stars being influenced by the core's rotation and mass.

This paper introduces a novel approach to independent component analysis, utilizing a specific type of divergence known as Arimoto-Harmonic-Matusita, which encompasses the well-known Hellinger-Matusita divergence as a special case. The proposed method, M-ar-K-FastICA, is a modification of the FastICA algorithm, incorporating the introduced divergence for optimization. Theoretical analysis confirms the method's validity, and numerical experiments demonstrate its superior performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to FastICA.

We revisit a classic connection between finite model theory and algebraic/proof complexity, focusing on graph isomorphism. We demonstrate that if a polynomial-time algorithm exists for distinguishing certain types of graphs using a specific property in the extended polynomial calculus, then this property can also identify non-isomorphic graphs efficiently, even when the graphs have limited connectivity. This finding implies that specific classes of graphs, including planar graphs and graphs with specific structural constraints, cannot be distinguished using a specific proof system, unless this system has significant limitations.
We have established an infinite set of $\sigma$-elementary rings, where each ring is defined by a finite collection of elements, denoted as $|\mathcal{R}|=\max\{3,\sigma+1\}$.

A common issue in online discussions is the presence of baseless assertions that cannot be disproven. These claims often serve as a means for individuals to evade accountability for their statements. To address this problem, we have developed a framework that identifies patterns within such assertions, thereby facilitating their categorization into distinct structural types. This framework is then utilized to analyze a vast collection of texts, revealing the prevalence of specific argument structures and providing insights into their characteristics.

This research introduces a novel approach to identifying spatio-temporal events from geotagged social media posts in real-time. By leveraging a combination of clustering, machine learning, and deep learning techniques, our method effectively filters out noise and accurately detects event occurrences across various locations and time periods. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a comprehensive evaluation on three real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to identify event occurrences with high precision and recall.

A new method is introduced to analyze the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure interactions through the bispectrum, utilizing the skewing technique. This method simplifies the process by breaking down the problem into two separate analyses: one involving the CMB lensing effect and the other, lens-free. The lensing effect is then incorporated into the final result through a straightforward combination of the two analyses. This approach significantly reduces the computational complexity, allowing for a more efficient analysis of high-resolution data sets. The method's accuracy is validated through tests on simulated data, and its application to real data is demonstrated using the Planck satellite and the Dark Energy Survey.

We've developed a new approach to Bayesian inference that guarantees accuracy in the face of potential data manipulation. This method is based on our earlier work that created a simplified model of complex data sets, allowing us to efficiently analyze uncertainty. By integrating this model with Bayesian techniques, we've created a framework that can learn and provide reliable estimates of potential data outcomes. Our results show that this method outperforms existing approaches in terms of both accuracy and resistance to data manipulation.

This study investigates the spread of online rumors in China during the COVID-19 pandemic, focusing on their characteristics, propagation patterns, and influential factors. A dataset comprising 1.2 million Weibo posts was analyzed, revealing that rumors tend to emerge from users with a moderate number of followers and spread rapidly within the first 24 hours. To better understand the dynamics of rumor propagation, we developed a model that incorporates the effects of public health interventions and found it to be consistent with observed data. Furthermore, we introduced a new metric to quantify the impact of individual users on rumor spread, which was validated through experiments. This research provides valuable insights into the nature of online rumors and their dissemination mechanisms, contributing to the development of effective strategies for rumor management.

The growing availability of high-resolution hyperspectral sensors has led to a significant increase in data volume, making it impractical to process the full spectral range for every application. This study investigates the impact of dimensionality reduction techniques on hyperspectral image classification, specifically examining the effects of reducing the spectral dimensionality. By comparing the performance of these methods on a dataset of 220 bands, we found that the choice of technique can significantly influence classification accuracy.

Recent advancements in NLP have been significantly propelled by the development of large-scale language models, which, however, come with substantial computational and storage requirements. To mitigate these challenges, this research introduces a novel compression technique for transformer-based language models, which is both model-agnostic and versatile in its application. The proposed method is based on a novel compression technique for continuous vectors, which is then utilized to compress the embedded layers and feed-forward networks within the transformer architecture. The results demonstrate that this approach can achieve up to 3.13x model size reduction with minimal performance loss of 0.11 F1 points on the GLUE benchmark, and even when regularized with dropout, it can attain a compression ratio of 2.06x with a performance loss of only 0.03 F1 points, outperforming existing compression methods in terms of efficiency and performance.

We've developed an innovative technique to validate and refine protein structures by leveraging high-precision quantum mechanical calculations of amide proton chemical shifts. By comparing these calculated values with experimentally obtained data, we can pinpoint inaccuracies in protein models and make targeted refinements. Our method successfully identifies structural discrepancies in the protein ubiquitin and further validates its results on the protein streptavidin.

Deep learning models heavily rely on the effectiveness of the loss function used to optimize their performance. This paper investigates the impact of different loss function types on the classification accuracy of deep learning models. We examine the suitability of loss functions designed for regression tasks when applied to classification problems. Our analysis reveals that loss function choice significantly influences model performance, with certain types yielding better results than others. We also found that the choice of loss function can affect the model's ability to generalize to unseen data. Our study provides valuable insights for researchers and practitioners in selecting the most appropriate loss function for their deep learning classification tasks.

We've developed a novel approach to parquet theory, viewing it as an exact decomposition of the Hamiltonian in terms of irreducible vertex functions. This vertex function can be expressed as an infinite series of effective interaction terms, which are derived from the Hamiltonian's action on specific subspaces. The approach is generalizable to various systems, including those with multiple bands and spin interactions, and is applicable to both conserving and non-conserving approximations.

We've created a theoretical framework to investigate the exciton condensation in two-dimensional layered materials, specifically applied to $\mathrm{TiSe_2}$. This model incorporates the effects of long-range Coulomb interactions in a self-consistent manner, treating excitons as bosons. Our results show that the model can reproduce the experimentally observed charge-density-wave transition in $\mathrm{TiSe_2}$, characterized by a temperature-dependent gap and the emergence of new spectral features at finite momentum. Furthermore, we've discovered that the model can also explain the finite momentum of the exciton condensate, which is a characteristic of the charge-density-wave state.

This research focuses on uncovering the hidden dynamics between users and dispatchers through their text-based communications in community safety reporting systems. By analyzing over 100,000 interactions from 10,000 users and dispatchers, we found that users and dispatchers have distinct communication styles and goals. Users tend to use more informal language and express emotions, while dispatchers use more structured and task-oriented language. Furthermore, we found that users' communication patterns are influenced by their personal characteristics and the nature of the issue they are reporting. Our study highlights the importance of understanding these interactions to improve the effectiveness of community safety reporting systems and the quality of service provided by dispatchers.

We've developed a theoretical framework to examine the magnetic properties of
triplet Cooper pairs in nematic superconductors, specifically focusing on the
exchange interaction between the spins of the paired electrons. Our analysis
reveals that the exchange interaction is anisotropic and its strength is influenced
by the superconducting gap's anisotropy. Furthermore, the magnetic susceptibility
exhibits distinct behaviors in both the normal and superconducting states, with the
nematic state's susceptibility being anisotropic.

This paper introduces Minimax Active Learning, a novel approach to minimizing the worst-case scenario of active learning by employing a minimax strategy. The method alternates between a learner and an adversary, with the learner querying unlabeled data and the adversary selecting the most challenging data points. Theoretical analysis reveals that Minimax Active Learning can achieve optimal performance in binary classification under the realizability assumption, and experimental results demonstrate its superiority over traditional active learning methods.

This research examines the evolution of music complexity from 1950 to 2015,
utilizing a statistical analysis of Western music recordings. By examining the
tempo and rhythmic patterns of 1,000 songs spanning various genres, we found that
the average complexity of these songs has been decreasing over time. Interestingly,
the study also revealed that the decline in complexity is not uniform across all
genres, with some experiencing a more pronounced decrease than others. Furthermore,
the research found that the decline in complexity is not solely due to the
increasing popularity of electronic dance music, but rather a broader trend affecting
all genres. By applying a mathematical model, we were able to quantify the
contribution of different factors to the decline in complexity, including the
increasing popularity of certain genres and the decreasing complexity of songs
within those genres. Overall, the study provides a comprehensive understanding of
the evolution of music complexity and highlights the importance of considering
multiple factors when analyzing this phenomenon.

A type of reinforcement process, which encompasses the classical Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz functional, is examined in this study. We derive key results, including laws of large numbers, asymptotic independence, and central limit theorems for this process.

This paper explores the concept of harmony within the framework of Computational Ludics, drawing parallels to the interplay of polarity and signs in Linear Logic's proof theory. We demonstrate that the fundamental properties of harmony in Computational Ludics can be derived from the interaction of polarity and signs.

A widely used approach to reward learning involves querying humans for feedback, but this method is costly due to its reliance on human input. In contrast, our proposed method, VACL, significantly reduces the time required for reward learning by leveraging visual information to group similar experiences and then asking humans for feedback on these groups. By utilizing visual data, VACL can effectively learn a reward function with fewer human queries, as demonstrated by our experiments on two simulated environments, which show that VACL can achieve comparable human performance with up to 10 times fewer queries.

We establish that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We investigate the properties of singular vorticities in two-dimensional ideal fluids, specifically focusing on a class of vortex structures with finite total vorticity and a characteristic rotational symmetry. This research extends previous work on symmetric vortex configurations by considering more general vorticities with a distinguished point, and includes a detailed examination of how these configurations evolve over time under the influence of the Euler equations. Notably, we establish the existence of solutions for all times for a broad class of initial conditions, and develop a framework for analyzing the stability of these vortex structures. This framework enables us to derive precise estimates for the behavior of these vortex configurations over time, and to demonstrate the persistence of their characteristic properties.

This paper introduces a novel approach to estimate the average treatment effect by combining neural network predictions with normalized augmented inverse probability weighting. The method leverages neural networks to approximate treatment models, which can be difficult to estimate accurately, especially when data is limited. By incorporating normalization and augmentation, the proposed estimator achieves superior performance, especially in scenarios involving high-dimensional covariates. Theoretical analysis confirms that the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and simulation studies demonstrate its improved efficiency over existing methods.

The $\tau$ lepton's unique properties make it an ideal subject for in-depth study, offering valuable insights into the Standard Model and potential new physics. Recent high-precision measurements from Belle II and other experiments have significantly advanced our understanding of $\tau$ physics, setting a new benchmark for theoretical predictions. This review provides an overview of the current state of $\tau$ physics, highlighting the latest experimental results from Belle II and other facilities, as well as the latest theoretical predictions from both lattice QCD and continuum methods.
